t: 3598. Longest Common Prefix Between Adjacent Strings After Removals — Editorial
o:
## Understanding the problem
For each index i, remove words[i] and report the longest common prefix (LCP) among adjacent pairs of the remaining array. Removing index i only destroys the adjacent pairs (i−1,i) and (i,i+1); all other adjacent LCPs survive. In example 1, removing index 1 or 2 destroys the run/run pair leaving no shared prefixes → 0; removing index 0 keeps run/run → 3.

With total length ≤ 10⁵, computing all adjacent LCPs once is cheap; answering each removal reduces to a range-maximum query over the adjacency-LCP array excluding up to two positions.
k: Removing index i only affects adjacencies i−1 and i; the answer is the max adjacent LCP outside those two.
Precompute prefix-max and suffix-max over the adjacent-LCP array for O(1) exclusion queries.
Total work is linear in the sum of string lengths.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force recompute per removal
a.i: For each i, rebuild the array without words[i] and scan adjacent pairs computing LCP from scratch. Simple and correct, but O(n · total length) — acceptable only for small inputs, shown for contrast.
s: For each i, iterate over consecutive pairs of the array with element i skipped.
Compute each pair's LCP character by character and track the maximum.
a.t: O(L) where L = total characters — building adjacent LCPs dominates; each query is O(1).
a.sp: O(n) for the adjacency and prefix/suffix arrays.

a.i: For tiny inputs, remove element i and scan all adjacent pairs directly. O(n·L) time; included to show the naive baseline the prefix/suffix method improves upon.
s: For each i, walk the array skipping index i.
Compute LCP of each consecutive surviving pair, take the max.
a.t: O(n · L) — recomputing all LCPs for each of n removals.

w: Always present the prefix/suffix-max solution; the brute force TLEs at n = 10⁵. Edge cases: n = 1 (answer [0]), n = 2 (both answers 0 since no pairs remain). Off-by-one danger: after removing i, the surviving adjacencies are exactly adj[0..i-2] and adj[i+1..]. Follow-up: support point updates to words with a segment tree over adj.
